newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy govt hunts for way to repair rift on Albania.
newsitem.headline: Italy govt hunts for way to repair rift on Albania.

text.p: Italy's ruling centre-left alliance on Sunday sought to salvage its credibility and mend potentially fatal rifts in its ranks over plans to lead a multinational security force into Albania.
At the centre of the row is Fausto Bertinotti, whose hard-left Communist Refoundation party's refuses to support the mission and shows little willingness to compromise.
Bertinotti told reporters his opposition to the mission remained unchanged, saying talk of a supplementary tax on Italians to pay for it was the "last straw".
Although Communist Refoundation is outside the government, Prodi relies on its support for a parliamentary majority.
He has summoned parliamentary party leaders of his alliance to a meeting on Monday ahead of twin votes this week to try to repair the worst threat to the survival of his his 11-month government.
Speaking to reporters in the northern city of Bologna, Prodi sought to appease dissenters by stressing that the U.N.-approved mission was a humanitarian rather than a military intervention.
That appeared to be enough for the Greens party, a member of Prodi's wobbly alliance, who have demanded guarantees about the scope of the mission before giving their full support.
Prodi is in no immediate danger in the votes on Tuesday and Wednesday as the centre-right opposition has given its backing.
But even government officials admitted that Italy's credibility was on the line as it prepares to lead its first multinational mission in post-war history.
The force, which will number up to 6,000 and assist international relief efforts after weeks of armed anarchy in Albania, is due to start deploying in the week of April 14.
"I'm not hiding the fact that the situation is very difficult and delicate because it involves Italy's credibility," cabinet undersecretary Enrico Micheli told Corriere della Sera.
Although Prodi has said his government will not fall over the issue, centre-right critics warned that the disintegration of the alliance meant it was now a lame duck and an embarrassment.
"Communist Refoundation doesn't vote, the government pretends nothing's wrong and it carries on as if nothing has happened," far-right leader Gianfranco Fini told La Repubblica.
"We'll cover ourselves in ridicule in the eyes of Europe and we'll also have proof of scant political seriousness in the current coalition."
Political sources said Prodi knows Italy has to pull off the Albania mission to be taken seriously in Europe.

Coalition members, already frustrated by Refoundation's refusal to countenance welfare spending cuts in Prodi's do-or-die drive to be ready for European economic and monetary union, heaped criticism on Bertinotti for his party's stance.
Massimo D'Alema, whose ex-communist Democratic Party of the Left is the biggest in Prodi's government, said it was a "a stunning display of political immaturity".
The coalition is split on whether a minority government could continue in office if Italy's dreams of finally achieving political stability would collapse and yet more elections would be needed.

Bertinotti said he did not mean to push Prodi to the brink. But he added: "What's at stake isn't our dissent over Albania, but something else. Maybe it's the fear of a real confrontation ...over the mother of all questions -- the welfare state...
"That's what the future of Prodi's government depends on."
